In patients with se- vere heart failure, addition of low-dose spironolactone to ACE inhibitors and loop diuretics reduced the risk of death or hospitalisation.48 Another aldosterone antagonist, epler- enone, has shown benefit49 in patients with heart failure Cardiovascular Drugs 1167 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) after myocardial infarction. Guidelines7,8,19 therefore rec- ommend that aldosterone antagonists may be added to standard therapy in patients with severe heart failure, and in patients with heart failure after myocardial infarction. In patients with less severe heart failure, their role remains to be established, although a small study50 has suggested that spironolactone may be of benefit. However, adverse ef- fects may limit use, and all patients taking spironolactone with ACE inhibitors must have their plasma-potassium concentrations closely monitored. Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin or digitoxin have an extremely long history in the management of heart failure. They are positive inotropes and increase the contractility of the heart thereby increasing cardiac output. Additional effects in heart failure appear to be due to neuroendocrine suppression such as inhibition of the sympathetic nervous system and indirect arterial vasodilatation. The benefit of cardiac glycosides in heart failure accompa- nied by atrial fibrillation is not disputed although beta blockers are generally preferred. However, their role in pa- tients with sinus rhythm has been debated. There is evi- dence that withdrawal of digoxin from patients taking diu- retics (the PROVED trial)51 or ACE inhibitors (the RADIANCE study)52 carries a considerable risk of clinical deterioration, and patients stable on such combinations should therefore be continued on them. However, the large DIG study53 found that, while addition of digoxin to diu- retics and ACE inhibitors improved symptoms, there was no effect on mortality, and a systematic review54 came to a similar conclusion. The role of digoxin therefore appears to be limited, although it may be used in patients who re- main symptomatic despite ACE inhibitor, diuretic, and beta-blocker therapy.5,7,8,19 Various vasodilators have been studied in heart failure. There appears to be no specific role for direct-acting vasodilators, but some benefit has been reported with a combination of isosorbide dinitrate and hydralazine.
